Restaurant Websites

Restaurant Website Design: 10 Features That Turn Visitors Into Diners

Planning a restaurant website? Here are the features that turn visitors into diners — mobile menus, online ordering, table booking, local SEO and speed.

NM Nipun Mitra ·26 October 2026 ·3 min read

A good restaurant website does one job: it turns someone who is hungry and curious into a booking, an order or a visit. Before choosing where to eat, most people search on their phone, glance at the menu and photos, check the opening hours, and decide within seconds. If your website is slow, hard to read or hides the menu in a PDF, they simply pick the next result.

Here are the ten features I’d include in any restaurant website, and the mistakes worth avoiding.

Why your restaurant needs its own website

Social pages and delivery apps are great for discovery, but you don’t own them. Delivery platforms take a commission on every order, algorithms decide who sees your posts, and you can’t control how your brand appears. Your own website is the one place where you set the menu, the prices and the experience — and where direct orders and bookings keep the full margin.

10 must-have restaurant website features

  1. A mobile-friendly menu in real HTML. PDFs are slow on phones, awkward to read and invisible to search engines. A proper menu page with sections, prices and dietary labels is better for diners and for Google.
  2. Opening hours, address and map — above the fold. These are the most searched details. Make them impossible to miss, including holiday hours.
  3. Tap-to-call and WhatsApp buttons. Many customers would rather message than fill in a form.
  4. Table reservations. A simple booking form that shows available times and confirms instantly by email or SMS. (I go deeper into this in my guide to booking website development.)
  5. Online ordering for pickup or delivery. Commission-free direct ordering is often the feature that pays for the whole website.
  6. Great, optimized photos. Food photography sells, but large images make pages crawl. Serve compressed, correctly sized images in modern formats.
  7. Reviews and social proof. Highlight your best reviews and link to your Google profile.
  8. Local SEO. Consistent name, address and phone everywhere, a complete Google Business Profile, and Restaurant structured data with your cuisine, hours and price range.
  9. Events, offers and private dining. Give people a reason to come back and a page to share.
  10. Speed. A hungry visitor on mobile data won’t wait. Aim for the page to be usable within two seconds.

Local SEO for restaurants

Most restaurant searches are local: “biryani near me”, “best café in Gulshan”, “rooftop restaurant Dhaka”. To show up:

  • Create a page for each location with its own address, hours and map.
  • Use your city and neighbourhood naturally in page titles and headings.
  • Add restaurant structured data so Google can show hours, price range and menu links.
  • Keep your Google Business Profile in sync with your website.
  • Make the site fast and mobile-friendly — both are ranking factors.

Common restaurant website mistakes

  • Menu only available as a PDF or an image.
  • Auto-playing video or music that slows everything down.
  • Outdated hours or prices that send customers to a closed door.
  • Booking or ordering buried three clicks deep.
  • No clear way to call or message.

WordPress or a custom build?

For a small restaurant that mainly needs a menu, hours and a contact page that staff can update themselves, WordPress is a sensible, affordable choice. If you want your own online ordering or reservation flow, integration with a POS, or top-tier performance, a custom build with Next.js and a small admin panel gives you more control and a faster site.

I’ve built WordPress websites and custom Next.js platforms, so I can recommend whichever genuinely fits your restaurant. If you’re planning a new restaurant website, get in touch and we’ll work out what will bring you the most diners.

Frequently asked questions

Does a restaurant really need its own website?

Yes. Social media and delivery apps are useful, but you do not control them and delivery apps take a commission on every order. Your own website is where you control your menu, take direct bookings and orders, and rank in local search.

What should a restaurant website include?

At minimum: a mobile-friendly menu in HTML (not just a PDF), opening hours, address with a map, phone and WhatsApp buttons, table reservations or online ordering, great photos, and local SEO with restaurant structured data.

Should I use WordPress or a custom build for a restaurant website?

WordPress is a good fit for a simple site that staff will update often. A custom Next.js build makes more sense when you need fast performance, your own ordering or booking flow, or integration with a POS system.
